book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook opens with the definition (reserve money / M0 = currency plus deposits with RBI) and then states the multiplier formula. Here the term is only announced with a teaser ('one becomes four'), then the video goes upstream to where the money comes from: who issues it, whether RBI can print without limit, the full-reserve ideal (anchored in the promise printed on every note), the reality of the Minimum Reserve System, and then the injection into banks. The multiplier is built by hand, round by round with one company's loan, summed to 2500, and only then named and given a formula, tested with a 10% what-if. The term high-powered money is explained last, with its reason (it is the money that multiplies). The order works because each answer raises the next question (can RBI print freely? where does the money go? why does it grow?), though the first half (printing rules) and the second half (multiplier) are only loosely joined.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Follow the rupee from its issuer to the banks: each stop gets one question (who issues it, how much may be issued, how it enters banks, what banks do with it), and the term is named only after the money's journey has shown why it deserves the name.

opening.what: Announces high-powered money, defines it in one line as the money RBI pushes into the banking sector, and teases that it multiplies 'one becomes four', promising to show how in this video.

narration.density: About 25 terms (high-powered money, reserve money, currency in circulation, issue, reserve, gold, foreign exchange reserves, ideal scenario, Minimum Reserve System, managed paper currency, rupee securities, treasury bills, repo, LTRO, MSF, OMO, reserve requirement, CRR, SLR, deposit, money supply, money multiplier, basic money, primary money, monetary base, M0) in about 600 s, about 2.5 per minute, but bunched: the first 230 s carry most of the new terms and dates, while the 230-560 s stretch spends five minutes on one worked example. The multiplier part suits a first look; the printing-rules part is fast for a beginner and makes factual claims that need checking.

talmel_summary: Picture and voice mostly land together, and when the picture leads it is by 2-5 s, often showing a step just before the voice explains it (deposit arrow, '+1000 reserves', four notes). The fit is strongest in the multiplier half: the loan arrow and the deposit arrow come back to the tray, each ledger row writes on with its spoken number, and the bend arrow shows 'it comes back' at the word 'vaapas'. Weaker in the printing-rules half, where rule sentences are written as small text and one label (Reserve Money on the injection arrow) is never spoken. Numbers that do not match: 98% shown but not spoken; the 150 + 50 crore what-if, the 1-2% cash share and the 10% → 10x → 10,000 what-if spoken but never drawn; the hook's four notes vs the computed 2.5x.

voice.notes: About 186 words per minute with almost no pauses (only two gaps over 0.7 s in ten minutes): fast, even and conversational. Teacher-like turns carry the structure: 'lekin', 'aap kahenge', 'ek baat bataiye', 'maan lijiye', 'ruk kar dekho', 'soch ke dekhiye'. Numbers are read plainly in rupees and crores (four hundred, two hundred forty, one forty-four; point seven eight), each spoken as it is written in the ledger. Stress falls on 'one becomes four', 'vaapas', and 'kitne saare transactions'. The idiom 'ek ka chaar' is used as a general word for multiplying, which clashes with the 2.5 result.

game_ideas.player_does: Plays the whole banking sector. RBI drops 1000 into the tray; each round the player drags the required share into the reserve vault and lends the rest to a company tower, then routes the company's spending to a shop that deposits it back.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each deposit comes back as a new row in the ledger and splits again; the reserve and loan totals grow, the lendable amount shrinks, and a money-supply meter climbs toward 2500 while a '2.5 X' badge fills.
game_ideas.win: Run the cycle until less than 1 rupee is left to lend, with reserves summing to 1000 and loans to 1500.
game_ideas.lose: Keeping less than 40% flashes an RBI penalty; lending more than is available bounces; letting a customer keep cash (a 'cash in pocket' slider) shows that money leaving the loop and the final total falling below 2500.
game_ideas.concept: deposit-loan cycle at a 40% reserve requirement

game_ideas.player_does: Sets RBI's reserve requirement with a slider (10%, 20%, 25%, 40%) to hit a target: turn an injected 1000 into exactly 5000 (or 4000, or 10,000).
game_ideas.process_happens: The ledger runs automatically, a dotted arc links the chosen percentage to the multiplier badge, and the formula 1 / ratio writes on with the result.
game_ideas.win: Hit each target money supply with the right ratio (20% for 5000, 25% for 4000, 10% for 10,000).
game_ideas.lose: A ratio set too high leaves banks short of loanable money (supply stops low); too low overshoots the target and an inflation gauge rises.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs RBI's printing press under three rule cards (full reserve; Minimum Reserve System 1956; the later 200 crore rule) and must fill the reserve vault with the right assets before printing notes.
game_ideas.process_happens: Under full reserve the press prints only as many notes as the vault holds; under the minimum system the press unlocks once the minimum is met and the backing gauge falls below 1%.
game_ideas.win: Print the requested notes without breaking the active rule card.
game_ideas.lose: Too little gold, or a vault short of the minimum, locks the press and shows which line of the rule failed. (Rule cards must use a verified source: the video's list of eligible assets is doubtful.)

checks_learned: A number in the hook must match the worked result: 'one becomes four' and four drawn notes against a computed 2.5x is a mismatch a check can catch (compare hook multipliers with the example's result).
Every spoken what-if with numbers (150 + 50 crore T-bills; 10% → 10x → 10,000; 1-2% cash) must also be drawn, and every on-screen number (98%) must be spoken.
Run a spell check on on-screen text before render ('held buy' for 'held by').
A formula with a percentage must be written in one consistent form (1 / 0.40 = 2.5, or 100 / 40) and evaluated by code against the worked example.
An iterative series must be computed by code (each round = previous lend x (1 - ratio)) and its column totals checked against the closed form (injected / ratio); here they match (1000, 1500, 2500).

Definitions and legal rules (what reserve money includes; which assets count toward the RBI minimum reserve; 'no real assets back the currency') must be checked against a source before they are spoken; flag absolute claims.
No promo overlay may cover content while the narration names it (M0 synonyms hidden at 594 s).
Real banknote close-ups and real signatures are replaced by BIE's own drawn note and promise line.
A label added to the picture should be spoken within a few seconds or not added (Reserve Money label at 249 s was never spoken there).

teaching_best.why: The learner's question 'can RBI print unlimited money?' is voiced before any rule, and the rule is then anchored in something every learner has seen: the promise printed on each note.
'Lekin ye sab kehne ki baatein hain': the ideal is stated, then overturned by reality on the same picture (= becomes ≠), so the Minimum Reserve System arrives as the real answer.
A question to the viewer ('what will the company do with its loan?') leads to the key insight that lent money returns as deposits, told as a short story of spending and depositing.
The multiplier is built by hand, round by round with one running number, and summed (1000 + 1500 = 2500) before the term and formula appear; the formula then confirms the hand result.
A what-if (10% gives 10x) right after the formula tests understanding and shows the inverse link between reserve ratio and multiplier.
The term announced at the start is re-explained at the end with its reason: it is 'high-powered' because it is the money that multiplies.

teaching_weak.why: The hook promises 'one becomes four' (and the closing says four or ten), but the video's own example gives 2.5; a learner may carry away the wrong number.

Reserve money is defined as all RBI notes except Re 1 and coins; the usual definition of reserve money (M0) is currency in circulation plus bankers' and other deposits with RBI. Describe, do not certify.
'Less than 1%' backing and 'no real assets back our currency' are stated as plain facts; RBI's actual gold and forex holdings are much larger than the legal minimum, so this needs checking.
Rupee securities and T-bills are said to count toward the 200 crore minimum (doubtful; the minimum is usually described as gold plus foreign securities), and the year of the cut is not given.
The 40% is called 'CRR and SLR'; the simple multiplier normally uses cash reserves, so mixing in SLR is a simplification left unexplained.
Cash held by the public, the main real-world brake on the multiplier, is mentioned twice and ignored, shown only as one text bullet.
No recap joining the two halves (printing rules and the multiplier); ends on a playlist plug.
